w-condition-invisible"/><div class="blog-image-overlay w-condition-invisible"></div></div></div></div></div></div></section></div><div class="all-blog-main-content"><section class="section_blog-content"><div class="padding-section-small padding-is_responsive-device top-margin-small"><div class="padding-global"><div class="container-large"><div class="main_blog-component"><div id="w-node-_5b477458-bc76-0e44-6e34-437a4c058fcd-c9d8d661" class="blog-article_main"><div class="blog-content-block"><div class="floating-date"><div class="date-number">22</div><div class="text-size-small">Aug 2022</div></div><div class="text-rich-text is-blog w-richtext"><h3>Introduction</h3><p>Last year provided further evidence that the cyber threat landscape remains both complex and challenging to predict. Between uncertain attribution, novel exploits and rapid malware developments, it is becoming harder to know where to focus security efforts. One of the largest surprises of 2021 was the re-emergence of the infamous Emotet botnet. This is an example of a campaign that ignored industry verticals or regions and seemingly targeted companies indiscriminately. Only 10 months after the Emotet takedown by law enforcement agencies in January, new Emotet activities in November were discovered by security researchers. These continued into the first quarter of 2022, a period which this blog will explore through findings from the Darktrace Threat Intel Unit. </p><p>Dating back to 2019, Emotet was known to deliver Trickbot payloads which ultimately deployed Ryuk ransomware strains on compromised devices. This interconnectivity highlighted the hydra-like nature of threat groups wherein eliminating one (even with full-scale law enforcement intervention) would not rule them out as a threat nor indicate that the threat landscape would be any more secure. </p><p>When Emotet resurged, as expected, one of the initial infection vectors involved leveraging existing Trickbot infrastructure. However, unlike the original attacks, it featured a brand new phishing campaign.</p><figure style="max-width:1960pxpx" class="w-richtext-align-fullwidth w-richtext-figure-type-image"><div><img alt="" src="https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/626ff4d25aca2edf4325ff97/68b885c2b3376168634e79d8_67ea7312984e601f71919603_6304aa12fbd531cd81579949_emotet%252520figure%2525201.avif" loading="lazy"/></div><figcaption>Figure 1: Distribution of observed Emotet activities across Darktrace deployments</figcaption></figure><p>Although similar to the original Emotet infections, the new wave of infections has been classified into two categories: Epochs 4 and 5. These had several key differences compared to Epochs 1 to 3. Within Darktrace’s global deployments, Emotet compromises associated to Epoch 4 appeared to be the most prevalent. Affected customer environments were seen within a large range of countries (Figure 1) and industry verticals such as manufacturing and supply chain, hospitality and travel, public administration, technology and telecoms and healthcare. Company demographics and size did not appear to be a targeting factor as affected customers had varying employee counts ranging from less than 250, to over 5000.</p><h3>Key differences between Epochs 1-3 vs 4-5</h3><p>Based on wider security research into the innerworkings of the Emotet exploits, several key differences were identified between Epochs 4/5 and its predecessors. The newer epochs used:</p><p>·       A different Microsoft document format (OLE vs XML-based).</p><p>·       A different encryption algorithm for communication. The new epochs used Elliptic Curve Cryptograph (ECC) [1] with public encryption keys contained in the C2 configuration file [2]. This was different from the previous Rivest-Shamir-Adleman (RSA) key encryption method.</p><p>·       Control Flow Flattening was used as an obfuscation technique to make detection and reverse engineering more difficult. This is done by hiding a program’s control flow [3].</p><p>·       New C2 infrastructure was observed as C2 communications were directed to over 230 unique IPs all associated to the new Epochs 4 and 5.</p><p>In addition to the new Epoch 4 and 5 features, Darktrace detected unsurprising similarities in those deployments affected by the renewed campaign. This included self-signed SSL connections to Emotet’s new infrastructure as well as malware spam activities to multiple rare external endpoints. Preceding these outbound communications, devices across multiple deployments were detected downloading Emotet-associated payloads (algorithmically generated DLL files).</p><h3>Emotet Resurgence Campaign</h3><figure style="max-width:902pxpx" class="w-richtext-align-fullwidth w-richtext-figure-type-image"><div><img alt="" src="https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/626ff4d25aca2edf4325ff97/68b885c2b3376168634e7a01_67ea7311984e601f719195d7_62fe6d8ab4e1dc31447ec032_Picture%2525201.avif" loading="lazy"/></div><figcaption>Figure 2: Darktrace’s Detection Timeline for Emotet Epoch 4 and 5 compromises</figcaption></figure><p><strong>1. Initial Compromise</strong></p><p>The initial point of entry for the resurgence activity was almost certainly via Trickbot infrastructure or a successful phishing attack (Figure 2). Following the initial intrusion, the malware strain begins to download payloads via macro-ladened files which are used to spawn PowerShell for subsequent malware downloads.</p><p>Following the downloads, malicious communication with Emotet’s C2 infrastructure was observed alongside activities from the spam module. Within Darktrace, key techniques were observed and documented below.</p><p><strong>2. Establish Foothold: Binary Dynamic-link library (.dll) with algorithmically generated filenames </strong></p><p>Emotet payloads are polymorphic and contain algorithmically generated filenames . Within deployments, HTTP GET requests involving a suspicious hostname, www[.]arkpp[.]com, and Emotet related samples such as those seen below were observed:</p><p>·       hpixQfCoJb0fS1.dll (SHA256 hash: 859a41b911688b00e104e9c474fc7aaf7b1f2d6e885e8d7fbf11347bc2e21eaa)</p><p>·       M0uZ6kd8hnzVUt2BNbRzRFjRoz08WFYfPj2.dll (SHA256 hash: 9fbd590cf65cbfb2b842d46d82e886e3acb5bfecfdb82afc22a5f95bda7dd804)</p><p>·       TpipJHHy7P.dll (SHA256 hash: 40060259d583b8cf83336bc50cc7a7d9e0a4de22b9a04e62ddc6ca5dedd6754b)</p><p>These DLL files likely represent the distribution of Emotet loaders which depends on windows processes such as rundll32[.]exe and regsvr32[.]exe to execute. </p><p><strong>3. Establish Foothold: Outbound SSL connections to Emotet C2 servers </strong></p><p>A clear network indicator of compromise for Emotet’s C2 communication involved self-signed SSL using certificate issuers and subjects which matched ‘CN=example[.]com,OU=IT Department,O=Global Security,L=London,ST=London,C=GB’ , and a common JA3 client fingerprint (72a589da586844d7f0818ce684948eea). The primary C2 communications were seen involving infrastructures classified as Epoch 4 rather than 5. Despite encryption in the communication content, network contextual connection details were sufficient for the detection of the C2 activities (Figure 3).</p><figure style="max-width:1073pxpx" class="w-richtext-align-fullwidth w-richtext-figure-type-image"><div><img alt="" src="https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/626ff4d25aca2edf4325ff97/68b885c2b3376168634e7a4a_67ea7313984e601f7191963f_6304af6ffbd5317d1657d1f9_Picture%2525201.avif" loading="lazy"/></div><figcaption>Figure 3: UI Model Breach logs on download and outbound SSL activities.</figcaption></figure><p><em>Outbound SSL and SMTP connections on TCP ports 25, 465, 587 </em></p><p>An anomalous user agent such as, ‘Microsoft Outlook 15.0’, was observed being used for SMTP connections with some subject lines of the outbound emails containing Base64-encoded strings. In addition, this JA3 client fingerprint (37cdab6ff1bd1c195bacb776c5213bf2) was commonly seen from the SSL connections. Based on the set of malware spam hostnames observed across at least 10 deployments, the majority of the TLDs were .jp, .com, .net, .mx, with the Japanese TLD being the most common (Figure 4).</p><figure style="max-width:1439pxpx" class="w-richtext-align-fullwidth w-richtext-figure-type-image"><div><img alt="" src="https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/626ff4d25aca2edf4325ff97/68b885c1b3376168634e79c8_67ea7311984e601f719195d0_6304afda0ef53f424636f0de_Picture%2525201.avif" loading="lazy"/></div><figcaption>Figure 4: Malware Spam TLDs observed in outbound SSL and SMTP</figcaption></figure><p> Plaintext spam content generated from the spam module were seen in PCAPs (Figure 5). Examples of clear phishing or spam indicators included 1) mismatched personal header and email headers, 2) unusual reply chain and recipient references in the subject line, and 3) suspicious compressed file attachments, e.g. Electronic form[.]zip.</p><figure style="max-width:627pxpx" class="w-richtext-align-fullwidth w-richtext-figure-type-image"><div><img alt="" src="https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/626ff4d25aca2edf4325ff97/68b885c2b3376168634e7a53_67ea7313984e601f71919642_6304b022471a7f43db414bf0_Picture%2525201.avif" loading="lazy"/></div><figcaption>Figure 5: Example of PCAP associated to SPAM Module</figcaption></figure><p><strong>4. Accomplish Mission</strong></p><p> The Emotet resurgence also showed through secondary compromises involving anomalous SMB drive writes related to CobaltStrike. This consistently included the following JA3 hash (72a589da586844d7f0818ce684948eea) seen in SSL activities as well as SMB writes involving the svchost.exe file.</p><h3>Darktrace Detection</h3><p> The key DETECT models used to identify Emotet Resurgence activities were focused on determining possible C2. These included:</p><p>·       Suspicious SSL Activity</p><p>·       Suspicious Self-Signed SSL</p><p>·       Rare External SSL Self-Signed</p><p>·       Possible Outbound Spam</p><p>File-focused models were also beneficial and included:</p><p>·       Zip or Gzip from Rare External Location</p><p>·       EXE from Rare External Location</p><p>Darktrace’s detection capabilities can also be shown through a sample of case studies identified during the Threat Research team’s investigations.</p><h3>Case Studies </h3><p>Darktrace’s detection of Emotet activities was not limited by industry verticals or company sizing. Although there were many similar features seen across the new epoch, each incident displayed varying techniques from the campaign. This is shown in two client environments below:</p><p>When investigating a large customer environment within the public administration sector, 16 different devices were detected making 52,536 SSL connections with the example[.]com issuer. Devices associated with this issuer were mainly seen breaching the same Self-Signed and Spam DETECT models. Although anomalous incoming octet-streams were observed prior to this SSL, there was no clear relation between the downloads and the Emotet C2 connections. Despite the total affected devices occupying only a small portion of the total network, Darktrace analysts were able to filter against the much larger network ‘noise’ and locate detailed evidence of compromise to notify the customer.</p><p>Darktrace also identified new Emotet activities in much smaller customer environments. Looking at a company in the healthcare and pharmaceutical sector, from mid-March 2022 a single internal device was detected making an HTTP GET request to the host arkpp[.]com involving the algorithmically-generated DLL, TpipJHHy7P.dll with the SHA256 hash: 40060259d583b8cf83336bc50cc7a7d9e0a4de22b9a04e62ddc6ca5dedd6754b (Figure 6). </p><figure style="max-width:1678pxpx" class="w-richtext-align-fullwidth w-richtext-figure-type-image"><div><img alt="" src="https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/626ff4d25aca2edf4325ff97/68b885c2b3376168634e7a4d_67ea7315984e601f71919668_6304b07ce54ef640ffeb3033_Picture%2525201.avif" loading="lazy"/></div><figcaption>Figure 6: A screenshot from VirusTotal, showing that the SHA256 hash has been flagged as malicious by other security vendors.</figcaption></figure><p>After the sample was downloaded, the device contacted a large number of endpoints that had never been contacted by devices on the network. The endpoints were contacted over ports 443, 8080, and 7080 involving Emotet related IOCs and the same SSL certificate mentioned previously. Malware spam activities were also observed during a similar timeframe.</p><p> The Emotet case studies above demonstrate how autonomous detection of an anomalous sequence of activities - without depending on conventional rules and signatures - can reveal significant threat activities. Though possible staged payloads were only seen in a proportion of the affected environments, the following outbound C2 and malware spam activities involving many endpoints and ports were sufficient for the detection of Emotet.</p><p> If present, in both instances Darktrace’s Autonomous Response technology, RESPOND, would recommend or implement surgical actions to precisely target activities associated with the staged payload downloads, outgoing C2 communications, and malware spam activities. Additionally, restriction to the devices’ normal pattern of life will prevent simultaneously occurring malicious activities while enabling the continuity of normal business operations.</p><h3> Conclusion </h3><p>·       The technical differences between past and present Emotet strains emphasizes the versatility of malicious threat actors and the need for a security solution that is not reliant on signatures.</p><p>·       Darktrace’s visibility and unique behavioral detection continues to provide visibility to network activities related to the novel Emotet strain without reliance on rules and signatures. Key examples include the C2 connections to new Emotet infrastructure.</p><p>·       Looking ahead, detection of C2 establishment using suspicious DLLs will prevent further propagation of the Emotet strains across networks.</p><p>·       Darktrace’s AI detection and response will outpace conventional post compromise research involving the analysis of Emotet strains through static and dynamic code analysis, followed by the implementation of rules and signatures.</p><p><em>Thanks to Paul Jennings and Hanah Darley for their contributions to this blog.</em></p><h3>Appendices</h3><p><strong>Model breaches</strong></p><p>·       Anomalous Connection / Anomalous SSL without SNI to New External </p><p>·       Anomalous Connection / Application Protocol on Uncommon Port </p><p>·       Anomalous Connection / Multiple Connections to New External TCP Port </p><p>·       Anomalous Connection / Multiple Failed Connections to Rare Endpoint </p><p>·       Anomalous Connection / Multiple HTTP POSTs to Rare Hostname </p><p>·       Anomalous Connection / Possible Outbound Spam </p><p>·       Anomalous Connection / Rare External SSL Self-Signed </p><p>·       Anomalous Connection / Repeated Rare External SSL Self-Signed      </p><p>·       Anomalous Connection / Suspicious Expired SSL </p><p>·       Anomalous Connection / Suspicious Self-Signed SSL</p><p>·       Anomalous File / Anomalous Octet Stream (No User Agent) </p><p>·       Anomalous File / Zip or Gzip from Rare External Location </p><p>·       Anomalous File / EXE from Rare External Location</p><p>·       Compromise / Agent Beacon to New Endpoint </p><p>·       Compromise / Beacon to Young Endpoint </p><p>·       Compromise / Beaconing Activity To External Rare </p><p>·       Compromise / New or Repeated to Unusual SSL Port </p><p>·       Compromise / Repeating Connections Over 4 Days </p><p>·       Compromise / Slow Beaconing Activity To External Rare </p><p>·       Compromise / SSL Beaconing to Rare Destination </p><p>·       Compromise / Suspicious Beaconing Behaviour </p><p>·       Compromise / Suspicious Spam Activity </p><p>·       Compromise / Suspicious SSL Activity </p><p>·       Compromise / Sustained SSL or HTTP Increase </p><p>·       Device / Initial Breach Chain Compromise </p><p>·       Device / Large Number of Connections to New Endpoints </p><p>·       Device / Long Agent Connection to New Endpoint </p><p>·       Device / New User Agent </p><p>·       Device / New User Agent and New IP </p><p>·       Device / SMB Session Bruteforce </p><p>·       Device / Suspicious Domain </p><p>·       Device / Suspicious SMB Scanning Activity </p><figure style="max-width:1120pxpx" class="w-richtext-align-fullwidth w-richtext-figure-type-image"><div><img alt="" class="heading-style-h2 _32pt b20">More in this series</h2><div class="w-dyn-list"><div class="w-dyn-empty"><div>No items found.</div></div></div></div></div><div class="related-blog_section"><div class="icon-embed-custom is-pixel w-embed"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="100%" height="100%" viewBox="0 0 8 8" fill="none" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" aria-hidden="true" </svg></div><div class="text-eyebrow">Continue reading</div><div class="eyebrow-reveal-div"></div></div><div class="spacer-medium"></div></div><div class="blog35_component"><div class="blog35_list-wrapper w-dyn-list"><div class="w-dyn-empty"><div>No items found.</div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div><section class="section_blogs-continued"><div class="padding-global"><div class="container-large"><div class="contiuned-blog-post-wrap hide"><div class="w-dyn-list"><div role="list" class="continue-reading-blogs-cl w-dyn-items"><div role="listitem" class="w-dyn-item"><div class="padding-section-small"><div class="blog-header"><div id="w-node-_6a4e4cbc-bd07-c860-591e-a3d80472f974-c9d8d661" class="blog-header-title"><div><div><div class="pixel-eyebrow_wrapper"><div class="icon-embed-custom w-embed"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="100%" height="100%" viewBox="0 0 8 8" fill="none" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" aria-hidden="true" role="img">
<rect width="8" height="8" fill="currentColor"/>
</svg></div><h2 class="text-eyebrow">Blog</h2><div class="text-eyebrow">/</div><h2 class="text-eyebrow">Network</h2><div class="text-eyebrow">/</div><h2 class="text-eyebrow">May 14, 2026</h2><div class="eyebrow-reveal-div"></div></div><div class="spacer-small"></div></div></div><h2 class="heading-style-h2">Chinese APT Campaign Targets Entities with Updated FDMTP Backdoor</h2></div><div id="w-node-_2561d5d9-fcb0-d673-7045-e0de5fb2172b-c9d8d661" class="blog-image-post-wrapper margin-0"><img src="https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/626ff4d25aca2edf4325ff97/6a035e9a22848bc92af31345_649aadc41cf6bc0827e47b69_GettyImages-1405668707.webp" loading="lazy" alt="" sizes="100vw" srcset="https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/626ff4d25aca2edf4325ff97/6a035e9a22848bc92af31345_649aadc41cf6bc0827e47b69_GettyImages-1405668707-p-500.webp 500w, https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/626ff4d25aca2edf4325ff97/6a035e9a22848bc92af31345_649aadc41cf6bc0827e47b69_GettyImages-1405668707.webp 724w" class="blog-header-image cover"/><img src="https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/626ff19cdd07d1258d49238d/62d845d8a4c357036c43d980_Blog%20Post%20Image.jpg" loading="lazy" alt="Default blog image" class="blog-header-image cover w-condition-invisible"/><img src="https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/626ff19cdd07d1258d49238d/62ad3aca1401273fd522699d_Photo.jpg" loading="lazy" alt="Default blog image" class="blog-header-image cover w-condition-invisible"/><div class="blog-image-overlay max-height-300"></div></div></div></div><div class="blog-article-grid"><div class="vertical align-left max-w-720 bottom-padding-40 bottom-border-grey"><div class="text-rich-text truncate is-blog w-richtext"><p>Darktrace have identified activity consistent with Chinese-nexus operations, a Twill Typhoon-linked campaign targeting customer environments, primarily within the Asia-Pacific &amp; Japan (APJ) region</p><p>Beginning in late September 2025, multiple affected hosts were observed making requests to domains impersonating content delivery networks (CDNs), including infrastructure masquerading as Yahoo- and Apple-affiliated services. Across these cases, Darktrace identified a consistent behavioral execution pattern: the retrieval of legitimate binaries alongside malicious Dynamic Link Libraries (DLLs), enabling sideloading and execution of a modular .NET-based Remote Access Trojan (RAT) framework.</p><p>The activity aligns with patterns described in Darktrace’s previous Chinese-nexus operations report, <a href="https://www.darktrace.com/resource/understanding-chinese-nexus-cyber-tradecraft" data-wf-native-id-path="c465d485-5c63-f62d-3089-c0491a89cdce_instance-0" data-wf-ao-click-engagement-tracking="true" data-wf-element-id="c465d485-5c63-f62d-3089-c0491a89cdce" data-wf-cms-context="%5B%7B%22collectionId%22%3A%22653a5c44bbd9309fc9d8d87e%22%2C%22itemId%22%3A%226a0356211421388bb15fe762%22%7D%5D">Crimson Echo</a>. In this case, observed modular intrusion chains built on legitimate software, and staged payload delivery. Threat actors retrieve legitimate binaries alongside configuration files and malicious DLLs to enable sideloading of a .NET-based RAT. </p><h2>Observed Campaign </h2><p>Across cases, the same ordered sequence appears: retrieval of a legitimate executable, (2) retrieval of a matching .config file, (3) retrieval of the malicious</p><p>DLL, (4) repeated DLL downloads over time, and (5) command-and-control (C2) communication. The .config file retrieves a malicious binary, while the legitimate binary provides a legitimate process to run it in. </p><p>Darktrace assesses with moderate confidence that this activity aligns with publicly reported Twill Typhoon tradecraft. The observed use of FDMTP, DLL sideloading, and overlapping infrastructure is consistent with previously observed operations, though not unique to a single actor. While initial access was not directly observed, previous Twill Typhoon campaigns have typically involved spear-phishing.</p><h2>What Darktrace Observed</h2><p>Since late September 2025, Darktrace has observed multiple customer environments making HTTP GET requests to infrastructure presenting as “CDN” endpoints for well-known platforms (including Yahoo and Apple lookalikes). Across cases, the affected hosts retrieved legitimate executables, then matching .config files (same base filename), then DLLs intended for sideloading. The sequencing of a legitimate binary + configuration + DLL  has been previously observed in campaigns linked to China-nexus threat actors.</p><p>In several cases, affected hosts also issued outbound requests to a /GetCluster endpoint, including the protocol=Dotnet-Tcpdmtp parameter. This activity was repeatedly followed by retrieval of DLL content that was subsequently used for search-order hijacking within legitimate processes.</p><p>In the September–October 2025 cases, Darktrace alerting commonly surfaced early-stage registration and C2 setup behaviors, followed by retrieval of a DLL (e.g., Client.dll) from the same external host, sometimes repeatedly over multiple days, consistent with establishing and maintaining the execution chain. </p><p>In April 2026, a finance-sector endpoint initiated a series of GET requests to yahoo-cdn[.]it[.]com, first fetching legitimate binaries (including vshost.exe and dfsvc.exe), then repeatedly retrieving associated configuration and DLL components (including dfsvc.exe.config and dnscfg.dll) over an 11-day window. The use of both Visual Studio hosting and OneClick (dfsvc.exe) paths are used to ensure the malware can run in the targeted environment.</p><h2>Technical Analysis</h2><h3>Initial staging and execution</h3><p>While the initial access method is unknown, Darktrace security researchers identified multiple archives containing the malware.</p><p>A representative example includes a ZIP archive (“test.zip”) containing:</p><ul role="list"><li>A legitimate executable: biz_render.exe (Sogou Pinyin IME)</li><li>A malicious DLL: browser_host.dll</li></ul><p>Contained within the zip archive named “test.zip” is the legitimate binary “biz_render.exe”, a popular Chinese Input Method Editor (IME) Sogou Pinyin.</p><p>Alongside the legitimate binary is a malicious DLL named “browser_host.dll”. As the legitimate binary loads a legitimate DLL named “browser_host.dll” via LoadLibraryExW, the malicious DLL has been named the same to sideload the malicious DLL into biz_render.exe. By supplying a malicious DLL with an identical name, the actor hijacks execution flow, enabling the payload to execute within a trusted process.</p><figure style="max-width:908pxpx" class="w-richtext-align-fullwidth w-richtext-figure-type-image"><div><img alt="" src="https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/626ff4d25aca2edf4325ff97/6a038a344b9c75656128ff2e_Screenshot%202026-05-12%20at%201.14.39%E2%80%AFPM.png" loading="lazy"/></div><figcaption>Figure 1: Biz_render.exe loading browser_host.dll.</figcaption></figure><p>The legitimate binary invokes the function GetBrowserManagerInstance from the sideloaded “browser_host.dll”, which then performs XOR-based decryption of embedded strings (key 0x90) to resolve and dynamically load mscoree.dll. </p><p>The DLL uses the Windows Common Language Runtime (CLR) to execute managed .NET code inside the process rather than relying solely on native binaries. During execution, the loader loads a payload directly into memory as .NET assemblies, enabling an in-memory execution.</p><h3>C2 Registration</h3><p>A GET request is made to:</p><p><code>GET /GetCluster?protocol=DotNet-TcpDmtp&amp;tag={0}&amp;uid={1}</code></p><p>with the custom header:</p><p><code>Verify_Token: Dmtp</code></p><p>This returns Base64-encoded and gzip-compressed IP addresses used for subsequent communication. </p><figure style="max-width:1192pxpx" class="w-richtext-align-fullwidth w-richtext-figure-type-image"><div><img alt="" src="https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/626ff4d25aca2edf4325ff97/6a038a8fbcb1e94021b99353_Screenshot%202026-05-12%20at%201.16.09%E2%80%AFPM.png" loading="lazy"/></div><figcaption>Figure 2: Decoded IPs.</figcaption></figure><h3>Staged payload retrieval</h3><p>Subsequent activity includes retrieval of multiple components from yahoo-cdn.it[.]com. The following GET requests are made:</p><p><code>/dfsvc.exe</code></p><p><code>/dnscfg.dll</code></p><p><code>/dfsvc.exe.config</code></p><p><code>/vhost.exe</code></p><p><code>/Microsoft.VisualStudio.HostingProcess.Utilities.Sync.dll</code></p><p><code>/config.etl</code></p><h3>ClickOnce and AppDomain hijacking</h3><p>Dfsvc.exe is the legitimate Windows ClickOnce Engine, part of the .NET framework used for updating ClickOnce Applications. Accompanying dfsvc.exe is a legitimate <code>dfsvc.exe.config </code>file that is used to store configuration data for the application. However, in this instance the malware has replaced the legitimate dfsvc.exe.config with the one retrieved from the server in: <code>C:\Windows\Microsoft.NET\Framework64\v4.0.30319. </code></p><p>Additionally, vhost.exe the legitimate Visual Studio hosting process is retrieved from the server, along with “Microsoft.VisualStudio.HostingProcess.Utilities.Sync.dll” and “config.etl”. The DLL is used to decrypt the AES encrypted payload in config.etl and load it. The encrypted payload is dnscfg.dll, which can be loaded into vshost instead of dfsvc, and may be used if the environment does not support .NET.</p><figure style="max-width:1430pxpx" class="w-richtext-align-fullwidth w-richtext-figure-type-image"><div><img alt="" src="https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/626ff4d25aca2edf4325ff97/6a038acf90fea8b031352c6a_Screenshot%202026-05-12%20at%201.17.16%E2%80%AFPM.png" loading="lazy"/></div><figcaption>Figure 3: ClickOnce configuration.</figcaption></figure><p>The malicious configuration disables logging, forces the application to load dnscfg.dll from the remote server, and uses a custom AppDomainManager to ensure the DLL is executed during initialization of dfsvc.exe. To ensure persistence, a scheduled task is added for %APPDATA%\Local\Microsoft\WindowsApps\dfsvc.exe.</p><h3>Core payload </h3><p>The DLL dnscfg.dll is a .NET binary named Client.TcpDmtp.dll. The payload is a heavily obfuscated backdoor that generates its logic at runtime and communicates with the command and control (C2) over custom TCP, DMTP (Duplex Message Transport Protocol) and appears to be an updated version of FDMTP to version 3.2.5.1</p><figure style="max-width:1426pxpx" class="w-richtext-align-fullwidth w-richtext-figure-type-image"><div><img alt="" src="https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/626ff4d25aca2edf4325ff97/6a038af099897b5807d56de0_Screenshot%202026-05-12%20at%201.17.50%E2%80%AFPM.png" loading="lazy"/></div><figcaption>Figure 4: InitializeNewDomain.</figcaption></figure><p>The payload:</p><ul role="list"><li>Uses cluster-based resolution (GetHostFromCluster)</li><li>Implements token validation</li><li>Enters a persistent execution loop (LoopMessage)</li><li>Supports structured remote tasking over DMTP</li></ul><p>Once connected, the malware enters a persistent loop (LoopMessage), enabling it to receive commands from the remote server.</p><figure style="max-width:1158pxpx" class="w-richtext-align-fullwidth w-richtext-figure-type-image"><div><img alt="" src="https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/626ff4d25aca2edf4325ff97/6a038b1326ed18ee42c79a23_Screenshot%202026-05-12%20at%201.18.24%E2%80%AFPM.png" loading="lazy"/></div><figcaption>Figure 5: DMTP Connect function.</figcaption></figure><p>Rather than referencing values directly, they are retrieved through containers that are resolved at runtime. String values are stored in an encrypted byte array (_0) and decrypted by a custom XOR-based string decryption routine (dcsoft). The lower 16 bits of the provided key are XORed with 0xA61D (42525) to derive the initial XOR key, while subsequent bits define the string length and offset into the encrypted byte array. Each character is reconstructed from two encrypted bytes and XORed with the incrementing key value, producing the plaintext string used by the payload.</p><figure style="max-width:740pxpx" class="w-richtext-align-fullwidth w-richtext-figure-type-image"><div><img alt="" src="https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/626ff4d25aca2edf4325ff97/6a038b385cc38f7dc4601667_Screenshot%202026-05-12%20at%201.18.58%E2%80%AFPM.png" loading="lazy"/></div><figcaption>Figure 6: Decrypted strings.</figcaption></figure><p>Embedded in the resources section are multiple compressed binaries, the majority of which are library files. The only exceptions are client.core.dll and client.dmtpframe.dll.</p><figure style="max-width:1114pxpx" class="w-richtext-align-fullwidth w-richtext-figure-type-image"><div><img alt="" src="https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/626ff4d25aca2edf4325ff97/6a038b5b432cfe66a60e1e34_Screenshot%202026-05-12%20at%201.19.36%E2%80%AFPM.png" loading="lazy"/></div><figcaption>Figure 7: Resources.</figcaption></figure><h3>Modular framework and plugins</h3><p>The payload embeds multiple compressed libraries, notably:</p><ul role="list"><li><code>client.core.dll</code></li><li><code>client.dmtpframe.dll</code></li></ul><p>Client.core.dll is a core library used for system profiling, C2 communication and plugin execution. The implant has the functionality to retrieve information including antivirus products, domain name, HWID, CLR version, administrator status, hardware details, network details, operating system, and user.</p><p> </p><figure style="max-width:728pxpx" class="w-richtext-align-fullwidth w-richtext-figure-type-image"><div><img alt="" src="https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/626ff4d25aca2edf4325ff97/6a038b8c7d6bc4c40e4c4ee2_Screenshot%202026-05-12%20at%201.20.25%E2%80%AFPM.png" loading="lazy"/></div><figcaption>Figure 8: Client.Core.Info functions.</figcaption></figure><p>Additionally, the component is responsible for loading plugins, with support for both binary and JSON-based plugin execution. This allows plugins to receive commands and parameters in different formats depending on the task being performed.</p><p>The framework handles details such as plugin hashes, method names, task identifiers, caller tracking, and argument processing, allowing plugins to be executed consistently within the environment. In addition to execution management, the library also provides plugins with access to common runtime functionality such as logging, communication, and process handling. </p><figure style="max-width:762pxpx" class="w-richtext-align-fullwidth w-richtext-figure-type-image"><div><img alt="" src="https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/626ff4d25aca2edf4325ff97/6a038ba50e139b3f4f31a12d_Screenshot%202026-05-12%20at%201.20.50%E2%80%AFPM.png" loading="lazy"/></div><figcaption>Figure 9: Client.core functions.</figcaption></figure><p>client.dmtpframe.dll handles:</p><ul role="list"><li>DMTP communication</li><li>Heartbeats and reconnection</li><li>Plugin persistence via registry:</li></ul><p>HKCU\Software\Microsoft\IME\{id}</p><p>Client.dmtpframe.dll is built on the TouchSocket DMTP networking library and continues to manage the remote plugins. The DLL implements remote communication features including heartbeat maintenance, reconnection handling, RPC-style messaging, SSL support, and token-based verification. The DLL also has the ability to add plugins to the registry under HKCU/Software/Microsoft/IME/{id} for persistence. </p><h3>Plugins observed</h3><p>While the full set of plugins remains unknown, researchers were able to identify four plugins, including:</p><ul role="list"><li><strong>Persist.WpTask.dll</strong> - used to create, remove and trigger scheduled Windows tasks remotely.</li><li><strong>Persist.registry.dll</strong> - used to manage registry persistence with the ability to create, and delete registry values, along with hidden persistence keys.</li><li><strong>Persist.extra.dll</strong> - used to load and persist the main framework.<strong>‍</strong></li><li><strong>Assist.dll</strong> - used to remotely retrieve files or commands, as well as manipulate system processes.</li></ul><figure style="max-width:1454pxpx" class="w-richtext-align-fullwidth w-richtext-figure-type-image"><div><img alt="" src="https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/626ff4d25aca2edf4325ff97/6a038bd1d12e0ebe5b29a885_Screenshot%202026-05-12%20at%201.21.32%E2%80%AFPM.png" loading="lazy"/></div><figcaption>Figure 10: Plugins stored in IME registry.</figcaption></figure><figure style="max-width:1444pxpx" class="w-richtext-align-fullwidth w-richtext-figure-type-image"><div><img alt="" src="https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/626ff4d25aca2edf4325ff97/6a038bf98673516ae8e6d2dd_Screenshot%202026-05-12%20at%201.22.14%E2%80%AFPM.png" loading="lazy"/></div><figcaption>Figure 11: Obfuscated script in plugin resources.</figcaption></figure><p>Persist.extra.dll is a module that is used to load a script “setup.log” to load and persist the main framework. Stored within the resources section of the binary is an obfuscated script that creates a .NET COM object that is added to the registry key HKCU\Software\Classes\TypeLib\ {9E175B61-F52A-11D8-B9A5-505054503030} \1.0\1\Win64 for persistence. After deobfuscating this script, another DLL is revealed named “WindowsBase.dll”.</p><figure style="max-width:1444pxpx" class="w-richtext-align-fullwidth w-richtext-figure-type-image"><div><img alt="" src="https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/626ff4d25aca2edf4325ff97/6a038c2584406f6db22d2b2f_Screenshot%202026-05-12%20at%201.22.57%E2%80%AFPM.png" loading="lazy"/></div><figcaption>Figure 12: Registry entry for script.</figcaption></figure><p>The binary checks in with icloud-cdn[.]net every five minutes, retrieves a version string, downloads an encrypted payload named checksum.bin, saves it locally as C:\ProgramData\USOShared\Logs\checksum.etl, decrypts it with AES using the hardcoded key POt_L[Bsh0=+@0a., and loads the decrypted assembly directly from memory via Assembly.Load(byte[]). The version.txt file acts as an update marker so it only re-downloads when the remote version changes, while the mutex prevents duplicate instances.</p><figure style="max-width:1224pxpx" class="w-richtext-align-fullwidth w-richtext-figure-type-image"><div><img alt="" src="https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/626ff4d25aca2edf4325ff97/6a038c4251290c6ec42c220a_Screenshot%202026-05-12%20at%201.23.26%E2%80%AFPM.png" loading="lazy"/></div><figcaption>Figure 13: USOShared/Logs.</figcaption></figure><p>Checksum.etl is decrypted with AES and loaded into memory, loading another .NET DLL named “Client.dll”. This binary is the same as “dnscfg.dll” mentioned at the start and allows the threat actors to update the main framework based on the version. </p><h2>Conclusion<strong> </strong></h2><p>Across cases, Darktrace consistently observed the following sequence: </p><ul role="list"><li>Retrieval of legitimate executables</li><li>Retrieval of DLLs for sideloading</li><li>C2 registration via /GetCluster</li></ul><p>This approach is consistent with broader China-nexus tradecraft. As outlined in Darktrace’s <em>Crimson Echo </em>report, the stable feature of this activity is behavioral. Infrastructure rotates and payloads can change, but the execution model persists. For defenders, the implication is straightforward: detection anchored to individual indicators will degrade quickly. Detection anchored to a behavioral sequence offer a far more durable approach.</p><p><em>Credit to Tara Gould (Malware Research Lead), Adam Potter (Senior Cyber Analyst), Emma Foulger (Global Threat Research Operations Lead), Nathaniel Jones (VP, Security &amp; AI Strategy)<br/></em></p><p><em>Edited by Ryan Traill (Content Manager)</em></p><p><em>‍</em><br/></p><h2>Appendices</h2><p>A detailed list of detection models and triggered indicators is provided alongside IoCs.</p><h3>Indicators of Compromise (IoCs)</h3><p>Test.zip - fc3959ebd35286a82c662dc81ca658cb</p><p>Dnscfg.dll - b2c8f1402d336963478f4c5bc36c961a</p><p>Client.TcpDmtp.dll - c52b4a16d93a44376f0407f1c06e0b</p><p>Browser_host.dll - c17f39d25def01d5c87615388925f45a</p><p>Client.DmtpFrame.dll - 482cc72e01dfa54f30efe4fefde5422d</p><p>Persist.Extra - 162F69FE29EB7DE12B684E979A446131</p><p>Persist.Registry - 067FBAD4D6905D6E13FDC19964C1EA52</p><p>Assist - 2CD781AB63A00CE5302ED844CFBECC27</p><p>Persist.WpTask - DF3437C88866C060B00468055E6FA146</p><p>Microsoft.VisualStudio.HostingProcess.Utilities.Sync.dll - c650a624455c5222906b60aac7e57d48</p><p>www.icloud-cdn[.]net</p><p>www.yahoo-cdn.it[.]com</p><p>154.223.58[.]142[AP8] [EF9] </p><h3>MITRE ATT&amp;CK Techniques</h3><p>T1106 – Native API</p><p>T1053.005 - Scheduled Task</p><p>T1546.16 - Component Object Model Hijacking</p><p>T1547.001 - Registry Run Keys</p><p>T1511.001 - Dynamic Link Library Injection</p><p>T1622 – Debugger Evasion</p><p>T1140 – Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information</p><p>T1574.001 - Hijack Execution Flow: DLL</p><p>T1620 – Reflective Code Loading</p><p>T1082 – System Information Discovery</p><p>T1007 – System Service Discovery</p><p>T1030 – System Owner/User Discovery</p><p>T1071.001 - Web Protocols</p><p>T1027.007 - Dynamic API Resolution </p><p>T1095 – Non-Application Layer Protocol</p><h3>Darktrace Model Alerts</h3><p>·      Compromise / Beaconing Activity To External Rare</p><p>·      Compromise / HTTP Beaconing to Rare Destination</p><p>·      Anomalous File / Script from Rare External Location</p><p>·      Compromise / Sustained SSL or HTTP Increase</p><p>·      Compromise / Agent Beacon to New Endpoint</p><p>·      Anomalous File / EXE from Rare External Location</p><p>·      Anomalous File / Multiple EXE from Rare External Locations</p><p>·      Compromise / Quick and Regular Windows HTTP Beaconing</p><p>·      Compromise / High Volume of Connections with Beacon Score</p><p>·      Anomalous File / Anomalous Octet Stream (No User Agent)</p><p>·      Compromise / Repeating Connections Over 4 Days</p><p>·      Device / Large Number of Model Alerts</p><p>·      Anomalous Connection / Multiple Connections to New External TCP Port</p><p>·      Compromise / Large Number of Suspicious Failed Connections</p><p>·      Anomalous Connection / Multiple Failed Connections to Rare Endpoint</p><p>·      Device / Increased External Connectivity</p></div><a data-wf-native-id-path="12e01b94-838a-455c-b1d7-11decc75142a_instance-0" class="glossary-item-orange-arrow show"/></a></div><div id="w-node-d1366120-05a2-bfd5-a9b0-2be9d20c7ad6-c9d8d661" class="vertical align-left"><div class="heading-style-h6">About the author</div><div class="spacer-medium"></div><div class="horizontal _20-col-gap"><img src="" loading="lazy" alt="" class="_80-square new-box-shadow w-condition-invisible w-dyn-bind-empty"/><div><div class="text-size-large">Tara Gould</div><div class="spacer-xsmall"></div><div class="text-eyebrow">Malware Research Lead</div></div></div></div></div></div><div role="listitem" class="w-dyn-item"><div class="padding-section-small"><div class="blog-header"><div id="w-node-_6a4e4cbc-bd07-c860-591e-a3d80472f974-c9d8d661" class="blog-header-title"><div><div><div class="pixel-eyebrow_wrapper"><div class="icon-embed-custom w-embed"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="100%" height="100%" viewBox="0 0 8 8" fill="none" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" aria-hidden="true" role="img">
<rect width="8" height="8" fill="currentColor"/>
</svg></div><h2 class="text-eyebrow">Blog</h2><div class="text-eyebrow">/</div><h2 class="text-eyebrow w-dyn-bind-empty"></h2><div class="text-eyebrow">/</div><h2 class="text-eyebrow">May 12, 2026</h2><div class="eyebrow-reveal-div"></div></div><div class="spacer-small"></div></div></div><h2 class="heading-style-h2">Resilience at the Speed of AI: Defending the Modern Campus with Darktrace</h2></div><div id="w-node-_2561d5d9-fcb0-d673-7045-e0de5fb2172b-c9d8d661" class="blog-image-post-wrapper margin-0"><img src="https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/626ff4d25aca2edf4325ff97/6a03236523b83451a1f4c848_images-2.jpg" loading="lazy" alt="" class="blog-header-image cover"/><img src="https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/626ff19cdd07d1258d49238d/62d845d8a4c357036c43d980_Blog%20Post%20Image.jpg" loading="lazy" alt="Default blog image" class="blog-header-image cover w-condition-invisible"/><img src="https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/626ff19cdd07d1258d49238d/62ad3aca1401273fd522699d_Photo.jpg" loading="lazy" alt="Default blog image" class="blog-header-image cover w-condition-invisible"/><div class="blog-image-overlay max-height-300"></div></div></div></div><div class="blog-article-grid"><div class="vertical align-left max-w-720 bottom-padding-40 bottom-border-grey"><div class="text-rich-text truncate is-blog w-richtext"><h2>Why higher education is a different cybersecurity battlefield</h2><p>After four decades in IT, now serving as both CIO and CISO, I’ve learned one simple truth: cybersecurity is never “done.” It’s a constant game of cat and mouse. Criminals evolve. Technologies advance. Regulations expand. But in higher education, the challenge is uniquely complex. </p><p>Unlike a bank or a military installation, we can’t lock down networks to a narrow set of approved applications. Higher education environments are open by design. Students collaborate globally, faculty conduct cutting-edge research, and administrators manage critical operations, all of which require seamless access to the internet, global networks, cloud platforms, and connected systems. </p><p>Combine that openness with expanding regulatory mandates and tight budgets, and the balancing act becomes clear.</p><p>Threat actors don’t operate under the same constraints. Often well-funded and sponsored by nation-states with significant resources, they’re increasingly organized, strategic, and innovative.</p><p>That sophistication shows up in the tactics we face every day, from social engineering and ransomware to AI-driven impersonation attacks. We’re dealing with massive volumes of data, countless signals, and a very small window between detection and damage. </p><p>No human team, no matter how talented or how numerous, can manually sift through that noise at the speed required.</p><h2>Discovering a force multiplier</h2><p>Nothing in cybersecurity is 100% foolproof. I never “set it and forget it.” But for institutions balancing rising threats and finite resources, the <a href="https://www.darktrace.com/platform" data-wf-native-id-path="7a721702-06ae-ef22-ef49-230662a51698_instance-1" data-wf-ao-click-engagement-tracking="true" data-wf-element-id="7a721702-06ae-ef22-ef49-230662a51698" data-wf-cms-context="%5B%7B%22collectionId%22%3A%22653a5c44bbd9309fc9d8d87e%22%2C%22itemId%22%3A%2269f39e5c0a9b13462a8916da%22%7D%5D">Darktrace ActiveAI Security Platform™ </a>offers something incredibly valuable: peace of mind through speed and scale.</p><p>It closes the gap between detection and response in a way humans can’t possibly match. At the speed of light, it can quarantine, investigate, and contain anomalous activity. </p><p>I’ve purchased and deployed Darktrace three separate times at three different institutions because I’ve seen firsthand what it can do and what it enables teams like mine to achieve.</p><p>I first encountered Darktrace while serving as CIO for a large multi-campus college system. What caught my attention was Darktrace&#x27;s Self-Learning AI, and its ability to learn what &quot;normal&quot; looked like across our network. Instead of relying solely on static signatures or rigid rules, Darktrace built a behavioral baseline unique to our environment and alerted us in real time when something simply didn’t look right.</p><p>In higher education, where strict lockdowns aren’t realistic, that behavioral model made all the difference. We deployed it across five campuses, and the impact was immediate. Operating 24/7, Darktrace surfaced threats in ways our team couldn’t replicate manually. </p><p>Over time, the Darktrace platform evolved alongside the changing threat landscape, expanding into intrusion prevention, cloud visibility, and email security. At subsequent institutions, including Washington College, Darktrace was one of my first strategic investments.</p><h2>Revealing the hidden threat other tools missed</h2><p>One of the most surprising investigations of my career involved a data leak. Leadership suspected sensitive information from high-level meetings was being exposed, but our traditional tools couldn’t provide any answers.</p><p>Using Darktrace’s deep network visibility, down to packet-level data, we traced unusual connections to our CCTV camera system, which had been configured with a manufacturer’s default password. A small group of employees had hacked into the CCTV cameras, accessed audio-enabled recordings from boardroom meetings, and stored copies locally. </p><p>No other tool in our environment could have surfaced those connections the way Darktrace did. It was a clear example of why using AI to deeply understand how your organization, systems, and tools normally behave, matters: threats and risks don’t always look the way we expect.</p><h2>Elevating a D-rating into a A-level security program</h2><p>When I arrived at my last CISO role, the institution had recently experienced a significant ransomware attack. Attackers located  data  which informed their setting  ransom demands to an amount they knew would likely result in payment. It was a sobering example of how calculated and strategic modern cybercriminals have become.</p><p>Third-party cyber ratings reflected that reality, with a  D rating. </p><p>To raise the bar, we implemented a comprehensive security program and integrated layered defenses; -deploying state of the art tools and methods-  across the environment, with Darktrace at its core.</p><p>After a 90-day learning period to establish our behavioral baseline, we transitioned the platform into fully autonomous mode. In a single 30-day span, Darktrace conducted more than 2,500 investigations and autonomously resolved 92% of all false positives.</p><p>For a small team, that’s transformative. Instead of drowning in alerts, my staff focused on less than  200 meaningful cases that warranted human review. </p><p>Today, we maintain a perfect A rating from third-party assessors and have remained cybersafe. </p><h2>Peace of mind isn’t about complacency</h2><p>The effect of Darktrace as a force multiplier has a real human impact. </p><p>With the time reclaimed through automation, we expanded community education programs and implemented simulated phishing exercises. Through sustained training and awareness efforts, we reduced social engineering susceptibility from nearly 45% to under 5%.</p><p>On a personal level, Darktrace allows me to sleep better at night and take time off knowing we have intelligent systems monitoring and responding around the clock. For any CIO or CISO carrying institutional risk on their shoulders, that matters.</p><h2>The next era: AI vs. AI</h2><p>A new chapter in cybersecurity is unfolding as adversaries leverage AI to enhance scale, speed, and believability. Phishing campaigns are more personalized, impersonation attempts are more precise, and deepfake video technology, including live video, is disturbingly authentic. At the same time, organizations are rapidly adopting AI across their own environments —from GenAI assistants to embedded tools to autonomous agents. These systems don’t operate within fixed rules. They act across email, cloud, SaaS, and identity systems, often with broad permissions, and their behavior can evolve over time in ways that are difficult to predict or control.</p><p>That creates a new kind of security challenge. It’s not just about defending against AI-powered threats but understanding and governing how AI behaves within your environment, including what it can access, how it acts, and where risk begins to emerge.</p><p> From my perspective, this is a natural next step for Darktrace. </p><p>Darktrace brings a level of maturity and behavioral understanding uniquely suited to the complexity of AI environments. Self-Learning AI learns the normal patterns of each business to interpret context, uncover subtle intent, and detect meaningful deviations without relying on predefined rules or signatures. Extending into securing AI by bringing real-time visibility and control to GenAI assistants, AI agents, development environments and Shadow AI, feels like the logical evolution of what Darktrace already does so well.</p><p>Just as importantly, Darktrace is already built for dynamic, cross-domain environments where risk doesn’t sit in a single tool or control plane. In higher education, activity already spans multiple systems and, with AI, that interconnection only accelerates. </p><p>Having deployed Darktrace multiple times, I have confidence it’s uniquely positioned to lead in this space and help organizations adopt AI with greater visibility and control.</p><h2>‍</h2><p>---</p><p>Since authoring this blog, Irving Bruckstein has transitioned to the role of Chief Executive Officer of the Cyberaigroup. </p></div><a data-wf-native-id-path="12e01b94-838a-455c-b1d7-11decc75142a_instance-1" data-wf-ao-click-engagement-tracking="true" author</div><div class="spacer-medium"></div><div class="horizontal _20-col-gap"><img src="https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/626ff4d25aca2edf4325ff97/63d1a5d3e7299476c5b4dea0_irvbruckstein.avif" CyberAIgroup</div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></section><section class="section_cta19 is-static"><div class="padding-global"><div class="container-medium"><div class="padding-section-large"><div class="pixel-eyebrow_wrapper"><div class="icon-embed-custom w-embed"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="100%" height="100%" viewBox="0 0 8 8" fill="none" const queryString = window.location.search;
  const urlParams = new URLSearchParams(queryString);
  const params = ['utm_campaign', 'utm_source', 'utm_content', 'utm_medium', 'utm_term', 'utm_id'];
  let url_additions = "";

  for (let param of params) {
    let paramData = urlParams.get(param) || localStorage.getItem(param) || "-";
    if (paramData) {
      if (paramData != "-") {
        url_additions += param + "=" + paramData + "&";
      }
      localStorage.setItem(param, paramData);

      // Select the form input by ID and set its value if it exists
      const inputElement = document.getElementById(param);
      if (inputElement) {
        inputElement.value = paramData;
      }
    }
  }

  url_additions = url_additions.slice(0, -1);  
  

const links = document.querySelectorAll('a');
links.forEach(link => {
    if ((link.href.includes('novalue') || link.href.includes('/virtual-innovation-launch')) && !link.href.includes('#')) {
        link.href = link.href + (link.href.includes('?') ? '&' : '?') + url_additions;
    }

 function addStates(whereto) {
    let states = [
      { "name": "", "code": "none" },
      { "name": "Alabama", "code": "AL" }, { "name": "Alaska", "code": "AK" }, { "name": "Arizona", "code": "AZ" },

      { "name": "Missouri", "code": "MO" }, { "name": "Montana", "code": "MT" }, { "name": "Nebraska", "code": "NE" },
      { "name": "Nevada", "code": "NV" }, { "name": "New Hampshire", "code": "NH" }, { "name": "New Jersey", "code": "NJ" },
      { "name": "New Mexico", "code": "NM" }, { "name": "New York", "code": "NY" }, { "name": "North Carolina", "code": "NC" },
      { "name": "North Dakota", "code": "ND" }, { "name": "Ohio", "code": "OH" }, { "name": "Oklahoma", "code": "OK" },
      { "name": "Oregon", "code": "OR" }, { "name": "Pennsylvania", "code": "PA" }, { "name": "Rhode Island", "code": "RI" },
      { "name": "South Carolina", "code": "SC" }, { "name": "South Dakota", "code": "SD" }, { "name": "Tennessee", "code": "TN" },
      { "name": "Texas", "code": "TX" }, { "name": "Utah", "code": "UT" }, { "name": "Vermont", "code": "VT" },
      { "name": "Virginia", "code": "VA" }, { "name": "Washington", "code": "WA" }, { "name": "West Virginia", "code": "WV" },
      { "name": "Wisconsin", "code": "WI" }, { "name": "Wyoming", "code": "WY" }
    ];
    
    // Populate the state dropdown
    for (var c = 0; c < states.length; c++) {
      if (c == 0) {
        $('[id=' + whereto + ']').append('<option value="-" selected>' + states[c].name + '</option>');
      } else {
        $('[id=' + whereto + ']').append('<option value="' + states[c].code + '">' + states[c].name + '</option>');
      }
    }
  }

  // Add states to any select with ID 'state' by default
  addStates('state');
  addCountries('country');

  // Function to handle change in country selection
  function handleCountryChange(event) {
    const countryValue = event.target.value;
    const stateElements = document.querySelectorAll('#state, [id$="-State"]'); // Selects all states including generic and form specific
    const stateBlockElements = document.querySelectorAll('#state-block, [id$="-State-Block"]'); // Selects all state blocks

    if (countryValue === "US") {
      stateBlockElements.forEach(element => element.style.display = "block");
      stateElements.forEach(element => element.value = null);
    } else {
      stateBlockElements.forEach(element => element.style.display = "none");
      stateElements.forEach(element => {
        element.required = false;
        element.selectedIndex = 0;
        element.value = "-";
      });
    }
  }

  // Attach event listener to any country dropdowns with ID 'country' or ending with '-Country'
  document.querySelectorAll('#country, [id$="-Country"]').forEach(countryElement => {
    countryElement.addEventListener('change', handleCountryChange);
  });

  // Webflow specific code to add states to forms listed in the array
  let forms = [
    "Start-Free-Trial", "Main-Form", "Nav-Get-a-Demo", "Primary-CTA-Free-Trial", 
    "Primary-CTA-Get-a-Demo", "Contact-Page", "Featured-Resource", "Whitepaper-Resource", 
    "Resource-Page", "Specific-Event-Form", "Specific-Resource"
  ];

  Webflow.push(function () {
    forms.forEach(form => {
      addCountries(form + "-Country");
      addStates(form + "-State");
    });
  });

  // Attach event listeners to all country dropdowns related to the forms listed
  forms.forEach((form) => {
    const countrySelector = `#${form}-Country`;
    document.querySelectorAll(countrySelector).forEach(countryElement => {
      countryElement.addEventListener("change", handleCountryChange);
    });
  });
var form = document.getElementById("main_form_2");
var url = window.location.pathname;
if (form){
  var field = form.querySelector("#Message");
  if(url === "/contact") {
    field.classList.remove('hidden')
  }else{
    field.value = "-"
    console.log("field.value", field.value)
  }
}

$('#current_url').val(window.location.pathname);
  
</script>

<script>
  const now = new Date();
  const dateTimeString = now.toISOString();
  $('form').each(function() {
   for (let param of params) {
    let paramData = urlParams.get(param) || localStorage.getItem(param) || "-";
 
     $(this).append($('<input>').attr({
      type: 'hidden',
      name: param,
      value: paramData
    }));
    
}
    $(this).append($('<input>').attr({
      type: 'hidden',
      name: 'currentDateTime',
      value: dateTimeString
    }));
    
    const formId = $(this).find('#form-identifier').attr('data-id');
    if(formId){
      $(this).append($('<input>').attr({
        type: 'hidden',
        name: 'form_id',
        value: formId
      }));
    }
  });
  
$('.form-label.focus-in').removeClass('focus-in');

$('.text-input, .select-field').on('focusin', function() {
  $(this).siblings('.form-label').addClass('focus-in');
});

$('.text-input, .select-field').on('focusout change', function() {
  $(this).siblings('.form-label').toggleClass('focus-in', $(this).val() !== '');
});
</script>
<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/gsap/3.11.4/gsap.min.js"></script>

<script>
let menuLink = $(".nav-dropdown-link");
let content = $(".nav-hover-2");
let menuBG = $(".nav-menu-bg-2");
let dropdownWrap = $(".nav-content-2");
let menuArrow = $(".nav-arrow-wrap");
content.hide()
menuBG.css("overflow","hidden");

gsap.defaults({
  duration: .3
});

function revealDropdown(currentLink, currentContent) {
  dropdownWrap.css("display", "flex");
  gsap.set(menuArrow, {
    width: currentLink.outerWidth(),
    x: currentLink.offset().left
  });
  gsap.set(menuBG, {
    width: currentContent.outerWidth(),
    height: currentContent.outerHeight()
  });
  gsap.set(content, {
    opacity: 0
  });
  gsap.set(currentContent, {
    opacity: 1,
    x: "0em"
  });
}

function switchDropdown(currentLink, previousContent, currentContent) { 
  gsap.to(menuArrow, {
    width: currentLink.outerWidth(),
    x: currentLink.offset().left
  });
  gsap.to(menuBG, {
    width: currentContent.outerWidth(),
    height: currentContent.outerHeight()
  });
  // invert moveDistance if needed
  let moveDistance = 10;
  if (currentContent.index() < previousContent.index()) {
    moveDistance = moveDistance * -1;
  }
  gsap.fromTo(
    previousContent,
    { opacity: 1, x: "0em" },
    {
      opacity: 0,
      x: moveDistance * -1 + "em",
      duration: .15,
        onComplete: () => {
            previousContent.hide()
        }
    }
  );
  gsap.fromTo(
    currentContent,
    { opacity: 0, x: moveDistance + "em" },
    {
      opacity: 1,
      x: "0em",
      duration: .15
    }
  );
}

let showDropdown = gsap.timeline({
  paused: true,
  onReverseComplete: () => {
    dropdownWrap.css("display", "none");
    menuLink.removeClass("active");
  }
});
showDropdown.from(dropdownWrap, { opacity: 0, rotateX: -10, duration: 0.2 }).to(menuArrow, { opacity: 1, duration: 0.2 }, "<");

menuLink.on("mouseenter", function () {
  menuBG.show()
  let previousLink = menuLink.filter(".active").removeClass("active");
  let currentLink = $(this).addClass("active");
  let previousContent = content.filter(".active").removeClass("active");
  let currentContent = content.eq($(this).index()).addClass("active");

    if(previousContent.length > 0 && currentContent[0] != previousContent[0]){
      setTimeout(function() {
        previousContent.hide();
      }, 150);
    }
	currentContent.show()

  showDropdown.play();
  if (previousLink.length === 0) {
    revealDropdown(currentLink, currentContent);
  } else if (previousLink.index() !== currentLink.index()) {
    switchDropdown(currentLink, previousContent, currentContent);
  }
});

$(".primary-nav-links").on("mouseleave", function () {
  showDropdown.reverse();
});

</script>

            return blockedDomains.includes(domain);
        }

        // Function to handle email input
        function handleEmailInput(event) {
            const email = event.target.value;
            const errorMessage = event.target.nextElementSibling;
            if (isBlockedDomain(email)) {
                errorMessage.style.display = 'block';
                event.target.setCustomValidity('Please use a business email.');
            } else {
                errorMessage.style.display = 'none';
                event.target.setCustomValidity('');
            }
        }

        // Function to handle form submission
        function handleFormSubmission(event) {
            const emailInputs = event.target.querySelectorAll('input[type="email"]');
            let formIsValid = true;
            emailInputs.forEach(input => {
                const email = input.value;
                if (isBlockedDomain(email)) {
                    const errorMessage = input.nextElementSibling;
                    errorMessage.style.display = 'block';
                    formIsValid = false;
                }
            });
            if (!formIsValid) {
                event.preventDefault();
            }
        }

        // Attach event listeners to all email inputs and forms on the page
        document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', () => {
            const emailInputs = document.querySelectorAll('input[type="email"]');
            emailInputs.forEach(input => {
                // Create an error message element
                const errorMessage = document.createElement('div');
                errorMessage.className = 'error-message';
                errorMessage.textContent = 'Please use a business email';
                input.insertAdjacentElement('afterend', errorMessage);

                // Add event listener
                input.addEventListener('input', handleEmailInput);
            });

            // Attach submit event listener to all forms
            const forms = document.querySelectorAll('form');
            forms.forEach(form => {
                form.addEventListener('submit', handleFormSubmission);
            });
        });
</script>


<script>
function updateLink(containerId, newHref) {
    const container = document.getElementById(containerId);
    if (container) {
        const dropdownToggle = container.querySelector('.navbar12_dropdown-toggle');
        if (dropdownToggle) {
            // Create a new anchor element
            const newLink = document.createElement('a');
            newLink.href = newHref;
            
            // Copy attributes from the dropdown toggle to the new link
            for (let i = 0; i < dropdownToggle.attributes.length; i++) {
                const attr = dropdownToggle.attributes[i];
                newLink.setAttribute(attr.name, attr.value);
            }
            
            // Copy the inner content
            newLink.innerHTML = dropdownToggle.innerHTML;
            
            // Replace the dropdown toggle with the new link
            dropdownToggle.parentNode.replaceChild(newLink, dropdownToggle);
        }
    }
}

// Call the function for each link
updateLink('products-link', '/products');
updateLink('resource-link', '/resources');
updateLink('company-link', '/company');
updateLink('partner-link', '/partners');
</script>


<script>
  // This script adds rel="noopener noreferrer" to all external links that open in a new tab (target="_blank")
  // Internal links (same domain) are excluded.

  document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () {
    const links = document.querySelectorAll('a[target="_blank"]');
    const currentHostname = window.location.hostname;

    links.forEach(link => {
      try {
        const linkHostname = new URL(link.href).hostname;

        // Skip if the link is internal
        if (linkHostname === currentHostname) return;

        // Get existing rel attribute or set to empty string
        let rel = link.getAttribute('rel') || '';

        // Add 'noopener' if not present
        if (!rel.includes('noopener')) rel += ' noopener';

        // Add 'noreferrer' if not present
        if (!rel.includes('noreferrer')) rel += ' noreferrer';

        // Set the updated rel attribute
        link.setAttribute('rel', rel.trim());
      } catch (e) {
        // Handle invalid URLs (e.g., mailto links)
        console.warn('Invalid URL:', link.href);
      }
    });
  });
</script>

<script>
   
  function shareToLinkedIn(btn, link) {
    btn.setAttribute('target', '_blank');
    btn.setAttribute(
        'href',
        `https://www.linkedin.com/sharing/share-offsite/?url=${link}`
    );
    btn.setAttribute('rel', 'noreferrer noopener');
}

    function socialShare(platform, btn, link) {
         if (platform === 'facebook') {
             shareToFacebook(btn, link);
         } else if (platform === 'twitter') {
             shareToTwitter(btn, link);
         } else if (platform === 'linkedin') {
             shareToLinkedIn(btn, link);
         }
     
    }
    
    // social sharing
    const btns = {
        'linkedin': document.querySelector('[data-social="linkedin"]'),
        'twitter': document.querySelector('[data-social="twitter"]')
    }

    const link = window.location.href;

    for (let key in btns) {
        if (btns.hasOwnProperty(key)) {
            socialShare(key, btns[key], link);
        }
    }
    
   </script>

<script>
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function () {
    function insertCTA(retries = 0) {
        let blogCta = document.querySelector('.blog-cta-report');
        if (!blogCta) {
            if (retries < 5) { // Prevents infinite retry loops
                console.warn(`CTA element not found. Retrying... (${retries + 1}/5)`);
                setTimeout(() => insertCTA(retries + 1), 500);
            } else {
                console.error("CTA element not found after multiple attempts.");
            }
            return;
        }

        // Hide the original CTA so it doesn't appear twice
        blogCta.style.display = 'none';

        document.querySelectorAll('.text-rich-text.is-blog').forEach(block => {
            let placeholders = [...block.getElementsByTagName("p")].filter(p => p.textContent.includes("[related-resource]")); // Uses textContent for security

            // Limit to inserting only 2 CTAs if multiple placeholders exist
            placeholders.slice(0, 2).forEach(placeholder => {
                let clonedCTA = blogCta.cloneNode(true);
                clonedCTA.style.removeProperty('display');
                clonedCTA.style.removeProperty('visibility');
                clonedCTA.classList.remove("w-condition-invisible");
                clonedCTA.classList.add("w-condition-visible");

                placeholder.replaceWith(clonedCTA);
            });
        });
    }

    // Run after Webflow scripts initialize
    window.Webflow ||= [];
    window.Webflow.push(insertCTA);
});
</script>
